toc.title: One: your safety isn't strong enough yet

sections.title: Focus on the small things you can do

toc.title: Three: you're using behavioral adaptations instead of feeling it
Four: you're judging it instead of allowing it

blocks.p: You're depressed. You've found and learned the Polyvagal Theory, and you know dorsal vagal shutdown is your dominant autonomic state. So you've started learning about coming out of shutdown, and you've even tried some stuff out. But nothing's changing. You're desperate, frustrated, maybe pissed off.
Let's look at what you might be doing "wrong," and why you're still stuck in shutdown.
The first thing to address is the question: are you keeping yourself stuck in shutdown?

I don't think someone gets stuck in shutdown randomly. No one chooses to be in shutdown. It's a fairly unpleasant state of affairs. And no one really chooses to remain stuck either. Day to day, it's not the most wholesome or fulfilling existence.

You're likely in shutdown in the first place because of things you've been through in your life, and most likely, I would bet, something to do with your upbringing. Shutdown often comes from a chronic disruption of connectedness, usually involving parents, or parenting, or a lack of parenting: parents who did not provide enough co-regulation, enough safety, enough predictability, enough love, and enough support. In my work as a therapist with teens and with adults, shutdown seems to often, if not always, be connected to past issues with family, upbringing, and parents. That can look many different ways, from outright abandonment to parents who just weren't emotionally available to connect with their children.

Shutdown can also come from ongoing, chronic, inescapable life circumstances. Poverty and neighborhood conditions can contribute to it. I don't think poverty equals shutdown, but it's a circumstance that contributes to the potential for shutdown. Neighborhood safety is another. So are domestic violence, chronic disease and illness, the death of a loved one, especially if that person was your safe person, and a whole bunch more. All of it can contribute to being in a shutdown state, even a chronic one.
Here I'm thinking more about the stuff from the past that has left you stuck in a shutdown state, like family or parenting, not the current life circumstances you might be stuck in.
So, did you cause your shutdown? No. But can you do something about it? Yeah, you can.

This isn't about blame. I'm not saying you're not doing well enough. I really hope this is more hopeful, more empowering. Empowerment is actually a really good word for it. When you come out of your shutdown state, the first thing you're likely to feel is flight or fight activation, and more likely fight: out of shutdown into fight, then flight, then up into safety, up your [Polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system). When we enter fight from shutdown, we want that to be an experience of empowerment.
But that only happens when you have enough safety in your system: when your ventral vagal safety pathways are strong enough to handle that returning sympathetic fight energy, and even welcome it.

blocks.h: One: your safety isn't strong enough yet

blocks.p: Right now, you may not have enough safety in your system. Again, it's not a fault or a blame thing. It might just be the way it is. Your ventral vagal pathways may not be developed or strengthened enough yet.

So as your body attempts to self-regulate out of shutdown into fight, it can be really overwhelming. The safety state needs to be developed more to welcome the sympathetic activation of flight and fight, especially fight at first.
Irene Lyon put it plainly when she was on the podcast:

q: You have been in shutdown and this depressed biological state. Coming out of that... is going to mean... all this stuff is going to bubble up and we're going to feel stuff that ain't that nice.

blocks.p: So the first thing you might be "doing wrong" is that your safety system probably just needs strengthening. I think that's a big part of this. It's foundational to how I work in therapy: do we have enough safety, and enough ability to feel our defensive activation, to come out of shutdown?
You need to practice being in safety before sitting with your shutdown experiences.

You might be trying to process the inner experience of being in shutdown: being depressed, alone, rejected, abandoned. You might be delving into the stories of your upbringing and the stuff you've been through.

If you're not ready for it, delving into that stuff can be retraumatizing. These things are super important, and eventually it might be very important to talk about them. But right now, and yesterday, and the day before, your safety state may not have been strong enough to handle that.

As you discuss the past, as you think about it and remember it, you're also going to feel it. On some level, you're going to flat out re-experience it. If your safety state isn't strong enough yet to welcome that with curiosity and compassion, it just reinforces the traumatized state of shutdown.

The next thing you might be doing is rejecting your shutdown state. This probably also stems from not having enough safety in your system. If you don't have the love and compassion necessary to welcome shutdown, which only comes from a strong enough safety state, you'll likely reject it.

As you come out of shutdown into fight, you might use that energy to reject the experience: to blame yourself, or maybe somebody else, but probably yourself. To shame yourself, to be mean to yourself in some way.

As we come out of shutdown into fight, we want to use that returning sympathetic energy to mobilize, and maybe be productive, or motivated, or just more physical in some way. We want to welcome it and use it. But if you can't welcome it with curiosity and compassion, that's when you lean into rejection, blame, shame, and negative thoughts.

blocks.h3: Focus on the small things you can do

blocks.p: So instead of judging yourself for what you haven't accomplished in life (maybe you've done that already, or will later: "I didn't do enough. I didn't do well enough at work. I wasn't a good enough spouse or parent"), focus on the small things you can do from shutdown.

I'm not saying give yourself a pass. Those thoughts can be valid, because you do want more, and that's okay. But I don't know how helpful it is to bash yourself for those things day after day. If you can do less of that, and focus more on the small things you actually can accomplish from shutdown, that might be more productive.

Maybe there are small, achievable things you can do every day. Maybe there are small changes to your routine that involve a bit more mindfulness, like starting your mornings with more slowness and more quiet. Focusing on the external environment. Connecting to it through your senses every morning. Listening for safety inside of yourself.

A small routine like that, with more mindfulness, from your safety and your shutdown state, is probably going to be more productive than using your fight energy to be mean to yourself, or using your shutdown lack of energy to be mean to yourself.

blocks.h: Three: you're using behavioral adaptations instead of feeling it

blocks.p: Eventually, we need to feel shutdown from safety, to allow it, and then to emerge out of it. Instead, you might be using behavioral adaptations.

From shutdown, you might be oversleeping. That's kind of a behavioral adaptation. You don't have much energy in shutdown, so it makes sense. But it's not mindfully experiencing shutdown, because you're asleep.

When coming out of shutdown, as that fight energy comes back into your system, you might be numbing it through doom scrolling: constantly on your phone, on social media, scrolling and scrolling, and you can't stop. I think a lot of people do that. Instead of feeling your shutdown, and feeling that returning fight energy, that mobilization, you're numbing it through doom scrolling, or other numbing behaviors or addictions, or maybe by being irritable and mean to others.
So you might not be feeling your shutdown or mindfully experiencing it. We need to allow it. Eventually. It might be too much right now, and that's fine. But eventually, it does need to be felt.

You need to embrace what it's like to be in shutdown, and that mindful experiencing gives your body permission to come out of it. Allowing shutdown will probably look like being quiet, being calm, and having lower stimulation. The way it looks for you might be different than for me, but that's generally what people are pulled toward.

If you're truly in a shutdown state and you don't give yourself that, you're not giving yourself the context, the environment, to mindfully experience shutdown. And if you're not mindfully experiencing it, you're just staying in it.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.h: Four: you're judging it instead of allowing it

blocks.p: One way you may not be feeling your shutdown mindfully is by judging it instead of allowing it.

You might be stuck in negative, pessimistic thoughts. These are very common from a shutdown state: projecting future failure, and dwelling on yourself as a present-moment failure and a past failure too. That's judging your shutdown, not allowing it.
When these thoughts come up, just notice them as best you can. Maybe say hi to them. Then focus on the present moment.

Those thoughts are there because story follows state. The thoughts of our mind come from the state we're in. So if you're stuck in a shutdown state, your thoughts are going to be flavored by shutdown, and they're going to reinforce the state. Those pessimistic thoughts make total sense. But they act as a top-down cue of danger that reinforces the shutdown.

I don't think it helps to dogpile on yourself about how horrible you are for having those thoughts. Instead, say, "Yeah, these are normal from shutdown. I see them. Hello." As best you can. Then focus on the external environment and try to reconnect with it, because the internal might be too much, or too numb. Connecting with the external environment might be more approachable.
Again, I'm not trying to blame you, or do my own dogpiling on top of what you're already doing to yourself. That's not the intention. It's not about blame. But it is about asking:

ul: What am I doing, even though it's unintentional?

blocks.p: It's not about blame, but I think it is helpful to say, "This is what I'm doing, and this is what I can do about it."
